_comment: The roster as data. Built 2026-08-15 from the restructure spec and signet-roster-system-v2.xlsx. Nothing about a booking is hardcoded in a page: act pages, roster cards, filter UI, per-act Offer schema and llms.txt all render from this file. The schema is deliberately flat and tag-based so it exports cleanly to the intranet/CRM later.
_presentation_note:
REVISED 2026-08-16 on Daniel's call, and this is the important axis. A first pass listed every act by name with a face attached, which meant inventing a flavour difference between Dan Steele and DF Funk that rested on a face chair the workbook itself marks 'assumed'. Daniel's correction: some of these are genuinely fronted and some are interchangeable, so do not name the interchangeable ones. Name them and you have promised a personality the booking cannot guarantee. Spec them and you have promised a sound, a size and a price, which is what you can actually deliver.

Two values:
  presentation: "face"  the person IS the product. Publishes name and face.
  presentation: "spec"  the format IS the product. Publishes instrumentation, never a name.

This is ORTHOGONAL to status (flagship/listing). Jazz Duo is a spec'd format with a full flagship page.
_img_shortage_note: REASSIGNED 2026-08-17. There are four placeholder stills for eight image slots: seven act cards plus the home page hero, which is img/hero.jpg. Collisions are therefore unavoidable and the only question is where they fall. The 17 Aug audit caught the worst one, the same trumpet on the Dirty Flamenco and Jazz Duo cards sitting side by side in the home page flagship grid. Assignment now: the three flagship cards and the hero are four different images, so the home page repeats nothing. What is left is Dirty Flamenco and the DJ sharing dj.jpg, one row apart in column three of the roster grid, which is the least visible pair available. None of these photos depicts the act it sits on; they are duotoned stock objects and the shoot replaces all of them, alt text included. UPDATE 2026-08-28: Dirty Flamenco's card now carries its own footage (see its _video_note), so the dj.jpg collision no longer renders anywhere; the img stays as data because the card falls back to it wherever the video field is ever cleared.
_source_note: The spec names signet-roster-final.xlsx as the content source. That file does not exist in the repo. The only roster workbook present is signet-roster-system-v2.xlsx, and this file is populated from its Roster and Chair Specs tabs.
_pricing_note: REWRITTEN 2026-09-04. This file carried the published rate card: a `denver` and a `resort` range on every rateCard row, an `hourly` on the duo, and per-config Offers derived from them. The site publishes no Signet price of any kind from that date, so the price columns are gone from the data as well as the copy; the repo is the published site and a number in a shipped JSON file is a published number. What is left is structure: the configuration ids, their labels and their piece counts, which is what the ladders, the roster filter and the schema still need. The internal card is in OFFER.md. Market figures live in _src/data/market-rates.json with their provenance and are the only figures any surface may render.
_scope_note: REFOCUSED 2026-08-17 for Q4. The 2026 product is small format: solo, duo, trio and quartet, cocktail through featured. Quartet is the published ceiling on every act and every surface. Five and six piece stays on the rate card under a by-request divider, because the published-pricing philosophy is the differentiator and hiding a number we hold would cost more than printing it; it is not merchandised as a standard product anywhere else. Seven, ten and thirteen piece are off the sold tables entirely (see site.json rates). Tejas Singh leads the roster and every featured-acts block.
_spelling_note: Tejas Singh, with the h. The restructure spec and the roster workbook both wrote 'Tejas Sing'; Daniel confirmed 2026-08-16 that the workbook was wrong, and it has been corrected at source. Do not 'fix' this back to match an older copy of the spec.
_players_note: No player names, no lineup, no 'collective of musicians' framing. On a face-led act the face is the one name published, because the face is what the client buys. On a spec'd format no person is named at all. Instrumentation is published everywhere, because it is part of the product; the people holding those chairs never are.

identity: One act, three sizes. This is the only booking on the roster that changes shape during the night instead of being replaced.

The reason to care is the contract. Most events buy the front of the night and the back of the night from two different acts, which means two load-ins, two sound checks, two sets of names to keep straight and a seam in the middle that guests can hear. This ladders instead: a duo through arrival and dinner, then the rhythm section arrives and the same voice fronts the dance floor. The party sees one band getting bigger.
At quartet it stops being a cocktail act. The full rhythm section behind one voice, keys or a second guitar on top, playing a covers set built for a floor.
It is a premium cover band. It is not a show band. Nobody changes costume, there is no choreography and there is no host segment. The band plays, reads the floor, and plays the next thing.
This is a named act, published under the name of the person who fronts it, and any substitution in the lineup is named to you in advance.

identity: This is the cocktail hour booking. Upright bass and guitar, playing the standards book, at a volume you can talk across.

It is sold as a format, with no name on it, and that is a deliberate promise. What you are buying for this hour is an instrumentation, a repertoire and a volume. Which two players deliver it does not change any of the three, and pretending otherwise would mean naming a pair we cannot guarantee for your date. You get the spec, on every date it is available.

Most of what goes wrong in the first two hours of an event is a volume decision, not a repertoire decision. A band that plays this hour at the level it plays the dance floor makes guests shout at each other while they are still deciding what kind of night it is. A duo is the honest instrument for it: two players cannot get loud by accident, and the arrangement stays open enough that conversation sits on top of it.
Standards are the repertoire because they are the one set of songs nobody has to be told about. Guests do not identify the tunes and do not need to. The night reads as expensive and unhurried.
The duo covers arrival, cocktails and dinner on one line of the contract. If the night also needs a dance floor, that is a second booking.

acts._video_note: LANDED 2026-08-28, the first real footage on the roster. Daniel's phone video from a live date ('monarch 1' in his archive): 53 seconds of the trio playing, guitar, bass and percussion, under the venue's uplights. Shot vertical with the 16:9 image letterboxed inside, so the black bars are cropped at the source and the published file is native 16:9; 99MB re-encoded to 14.5MB, H.264, faststart. acts.blurb: Brilliant, guitar-based flamenco musical act and one of the only ones in Colorado available for private event bookings. Dirty flamenco plays real palos, and rhumba both authentically and with a soulful twist. They are a polished, working group with an extensive standing repertoire.
acts.seo_title: Dirty Flamenco: flamenco trio for private events in Denver
acts.meta_description: Flamenco for weddings, corporate dinners and private events in Denver and the Colorado mountains. Trio, or a quartet with a dancer for a program that wants a set piece.
identity: Flamenco is the booking on this roster that almost nobody else in Colorado sells as a private event product. It exists here as a concert act, or as a guitarist playing Spanish-flavored background. Dirty Flamenco is neither. It is a working group with a standing repertoire, sold at private event scale.

Most live music at a private event is designed to be felt and not watched. This is the opposite booking, and its work is the set moment: a cultural centerpiece, a corporate dinner that has to be memorable, a reception that wants something guests will describe to people who were not there.

The repertoire is palos, the traditional forms, not a set of pop songs with nylon strings on them. That is the difference between a flamenco booking and a Spanish guitar booking, and it is audible inside eight bars.
This is a named act rather than a format, an existing group booked under its own name. Any change to the lineup is named to you in advance.

ladder.bestFor: Cocktails and dinner. Full volume range without a dance floor.
A program with a set piece in it.

setlist.note: Flamenco is organized by palo, the traditional form, rather than by song title. A set is built from these and shaped to the crowd on the night. Representative, not fixed.

identity: Last Consulate is the solo project of one multi-instrumentalist, built on upright bass, electric bass, guitar and downtempo electronics.

The improvising is jazz. The production is early-2000s downtempo electronica, the slow and hazy end of it, instrumental and warm, and mixed so that what was played and what was sampled are hard to tell apart.
Upright bass is the lead instrument. Under it sit slow hip-hop drums, extended jazz harmony, tape-worn keys and delayed guitars, and the improvised bass line is usually the melody.
It is built for arrival, cocktails and dinner, played at a volume guests can talk across, with the feel of a late jazz set or a hotel lobby.
